items.title: PCE Inflation Holds at 3.3% Ahead of Fed Chair Warsh's First Jackson Hole Speech
items.body:
## A Data Point With Unusually High Stakes

Wednesday's release of the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index — the inflation gauge the Federal Reserve says it watches most closely — landed with unusually high stakes attached. Core PCE, which strips out volatile food and energy prices, came in at 3.3% on a year-over-year basis, matching the prior month's pace rather than accelerating or cooling meaningfully.

The timing is what turned an otherwise routine data release into a market-moving event. Two days later, Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh is scheduled to deliver his first keynote address at the Kansas City Fed's Jackson Hole Economic Symposium since taking the helm of the central bank — a venue that recent Fed chairs have used to signal major shifts in policy thinking. Investors were always going to parse that speech line by line. Now they have a fresh inflation print to measure it against.

## What The Report Actually Showed

According to the Commerce Department's Bureau of Economic Analysis, headline PCE inflation and the core reading both remained above the Fed's long-standing 2% target. A few points stood out to economists reviewing the release:

- **Core PCE held steady** at 3.3% year-over-year, suggesting underlying price pressure has plateaued rather than resumed climbing — but also has not resumed its earlier descent toward target.
- **Personal income and spending** figures released alongside the price data pointed to a consumer that is still spending, though at a more measured pace than earlier in the cycle.
- **Services inflation**, which has been the stickiest component of the basket in recent years, appears to be the primary reason the overall figure has stalled rather than fallen further.

None of this amounts to a dramatic surprise in either direction. That, in itself, is the story: a "3.3% and steady" print gives policymakers no clean excuse to declare victory over inflation, but also no fresh alarm bell to justify holding rates higher for longer.

## Why Markets Are Fixated on September

Futures markets have spent recent weeks pricing in a meaningful probability that the Fed cuts its benchmark rate at the September meeting. A print like this one — neither hot enough to derail that expectation nor cool enough to cement it — tends to keep traders exactly where they were before the data dropped: leaning toward a cut, but not fully committed.

That ambiguity is precisely why Chair Warsh's Jackson Hole remarks carry extra weight this year. A debut keynote from a new Fed chair is typically read as a signal-setting moment regardless of circumstance. Coming just 48 hours after an inflation report that resolved nothing, it becomes the tie-breaker markets are waiting on. Analysts caution that a single speech rarely commits a data-dependent Fed to a specific decision weeks in advance, but the framing, tone, and emphasis Warsh chooses — on labor market slack, on services inflation, on the risks of moving too early versus too late — will likely shape how confidently traders position ahead of the September Federal Open Market Committee meeting.

## The Balancing Act Facing a New Chair

Any incoming Fed chair inherits a communication challenge: markets look for continuity with prior policy frameworks while also watching for hints of a distinct approach. That challenge is sharper when the first major public address follows an inflation report that essentially punts the hardest questions.

Fed watchers will likely be listening for a few specific signals in the speech itself:

1. **Language around "sufficiently restrictive"** policy — whether Warsh characterizes current rates as still needed to cool the economy or as increasingly ready to ease.
2. **Emphasis on the labor market** relative to inflation — a pivot toward employment risks is often read as more dovish.
3. **Any reference to the "last mile" problem** — the well-documented pattern of inflation cooling quickly from very high levels but stalling before reaching target.

## What Comes Next

Between now and the September FOMC decision, additional employment and inflation data will arrive and could shift the calculus further in either direction — a reminder that a single PCE report or a single speech rarely tells the whole story. Markets tend to treat Jackson Hole remarks as directional guidance rather than a binding pre-commitment, and Fed officials have historically preserved optionality until the meeting itself.

For now, the takeaway from Wednesday's data is narrower than headlines might suggest: inflation is not accelerating, but it is not resuming its decline either. That leaves the September decision genuinely open — and puts real weight on how Chair Warsh chooses to frame the path forward when he steps to the podium at Jackson Hole.

*This article is for informational purposes only and does not constitute financial, investment, or trading advice. Economic data and Federal Reserve policy expectations can change quickly; readers should consult official sources and licensed financial advisors before making investment decisions.*

items.title: A Tanker Strike Off Oman, a Delegation in Tehran: Why a Hormuz Ceasefire Still Isn't Close
items.body:
## A Fragile Diplomatic Window, Shattered Within Hours

Just hours after a Pakistani delegation concluded a fresh round of talks in Tehran aimed at ending nearly six months of conflict around the Strait of Hormuz, another commercial tanker was struck off the coast of Oman. The timing was jarring: diplomats had barely left the room before the waterway reminded the world why a durable ceasefire remains elusive.

According to shipping-industry monitors and regional officials, the vessel was transiting international waters near Omani territory when it sustained damage consistent with previous attacks reported in the strait over recent months. No group has been formally confirmed as responsible, and assessments of the incident are still being verified by maritime security firms and flag-state authorities.

## Why the Strait Matters So Much

The Strait of Hormuz is one of the world's most critical chokepoints, with a large share of globally traded crude oil and liquefied natural gas passing through its narrow channel every day. Even the perception of heightened risk there tends to ripple outward — nudging up tanker insurance premiums, prompting shipping lines to reroute or pause transits, and adding volatility to energy markets far from the Gulf itself.

That is part of why, six months into the conflict, regional and international actors have kept pushing for a negotiated de-escalation even as fighting continues. A prolonged disruption to Hormuz traffic carries costs that extend well beyond the countries directly involved.

## Islamabad's Quiet Mediation Role

Pakistan's involvement reflects its unusual position: it maintains working relationships with multiple parties to the conflict and has domestic economic incentives — from energy imports to regional trade routes — in seeing the crisis contained. The Tehran talks were described by people familiar with the discussions as focused on confidence-building measures rather than a comprehensive settlement: steps such as protected shipping corridors, communication hotlines to prevent miscalculation, and a phased de-escalation framework.

Diplomats involved in similar past mediation efforts caution that this kind of shuttle diplomacy rarely produces an immediate breakthrough. Instead, it tends to lay groundwork — testing whether the parties are willing to accept even limited, verifiable steps before broader negotiations become possible.

## The Gap Between the Table and the Water

The tanker strike underscores a persistent problem in conflicts fought partly at sea: control over irregular or proxy actors is often looser than it is on land, and a single incident can undercut weeks of diplomatic groundwork. Analysts tracking the conflict note that attacks near shipping lanes have repeatedly coincided with periods of active negotiation, raising questions about whether all relevant factions are equally committed to a pause — or whether some see continued pressure on shipping as useful leverage at the table.

For now, maritime authorities have reiterated advisories urging vessels transiting the strait to maintain heightened vigilance, follow recommended security corridors, and report any unusual activity promptly.

## What Comes Next

Officials involved in the talks have not announced a timeline for a follow-up round, though regional diplomats suggest further contacts are likely given the economic stakes for all sides. Markets and shipping firms, meanwhile, are left watching an uneasy space between negotiation and disruption — where progress in Tehran's meeting rooms has yet to translate into calm on the water.

Until that gap closes, incidents like the latest strike off Oman are likely to remain a recurring test of whether the six-month conflict is nearing an end or simply entering its next uncertain phase.

*This article is a news summary and analysis based on publicly reported developments. Details of individual incidents may be revised as official investigations and verified reporting become available.*

items.title: 281 Dead, 12,000 Homes Gone: Inside Colombia's Search for the Missing After Its Worst Quake in a Century
items.body:
More than two weeks after the ground shook western Colombia to its core, rescue teams are still working through collapsed neighborhoods, hoping to find survivors — or at least answers — for the hundreds of families still waiting for news of missing loved ones.

## What happened

On August 10, 2026, a magnitude-7.4 earthquake struck near the town of San José del Palmar in Colombia's Chocó department, one of the country's poorest and most remote regions. The quake was followed by a series of aftershocks, some strong enough to bring down already-weakened buildings, and was quickly described by seismologists as the most powerful to hit Colombia in the 21st century.

The shaking reached far beyond the epicenter. Cities including Cali, Pereira, Quibdó, and Manizales all reported serious damage, from cracked apartment blocks to full building collapses. Cali, one of Colombia's largest cities, has emerged as the hardest-hit urban center, with local officials reporting dozens of deaths and well over a thousand injuries within the city alone.

## A death toll still climbing

According to Colombia's national disaster management agency, UNGRD, the confirmed death toll has climbed steadily since the quake first hit, standing at 281 in the latest official count. Thousands more were injured, and several hundred people remain listed as missing — a number that has only slowly come down as search crews work through debris in hard-hit towns.

Search and rescue operations have been complicated by the terrain itself. Much of Chocó is dense jungle and mountainous countryside with few paved roads, and landslides triggered by the quake and its aftershocks blocked several routes that rescue convoys needed to reach isolated villages. In the days immediately after the disaster, some communities were reachable only by helicopter or on foot.

## Tens of thousands without homes

The material toll has been staggering. Government estimates put the number of destroyed homes above 12,000, with tens of thousands more damaged to the point of being unsafe to occupy. Officials say the earthquake has affected people across more than a dozen departments and hundreds of municipalities, leaving tens of thousands of Colombians displaced and in need of emergency shelter.

In the hardest-hit towns, temporary camps of tents and tarps have gone up in plazas, schoolyards, and open fields, as families who lost their homes wait for word on longer-term housing. Aid groups and government agencies have been distributing food, water, and medical supplies, though officials have acknowledged that reaching the most remote communities remains a challenge weeks into the response.

## The road ahead

Colombia's government has pledged support for reconstruction in the affected departments, and international aid organizations have joined the response alongside national agencies. But with so many communities still cut off by damaged infrastructure, and with search teams still combing through rubble for the missing, officials have been cautious about predicting when the recovery phase will fully take over from the search-and-rescue effort.

For families in Chocó, Valle del Cauca, and the other affected regions, the earthquake's immediate danger may have passed, but the harder task — rebuilding towns, tracing the missing, and finding permanent shelter for tens of thousands of people — is only just beginning.
